title: Satellites caught these dunes moving
subtitle: Sperrgebiet · southern Namib · Namibia
deck: Watch a dune for a minute and it looks eternal. Watch the same corridor year by year and the crescents march. Landsat does not argue — it overlays the evidence.
shortDescription: Registered Landsat frames show Namib barchans migrating north — measured in meters per year.
seoTitle: Satellites Caught These Dunes Moving — Namib Migration Explained — Deep Forest Dispatch
metaDescription: Landsat time series shows Sperrgebiet dunes in Namibia migrating meters per year — how satellites prove motion and how dunes actually advance.

hero.alt: Landsat view of barchan and transverse dunes in the Sperrgebiet, southern Namib Desert, from the 2022 end of a registered time series
hero.credit: NASA Earth Observatory · Landsat 8/9 sequence (Racing Dunes)

blocks.html: In Namibia’s Sperrgebiet — the southern Namib — crescent barchans and transverse ridges sit in a fierce south-to-southwest wind corridor. NASA Earth Observatory assembled annual Landsat 8 and 9 scenes from 2013 to 2022. Drag the handle: the dunes do not stay put.

before.alt: Landsat frame of Sperrgebiet dunes circa 2013 from NASA Racing Dunes sequence

after.alt: Landsat frame of the same Sperrgebiet corridor circa 2022 showing northward dune migration

blocks.caption: Registered Landsat corridor from NASA EO “Racing Dunes in Namibia” — first and last frames of the 2013–2022 annual sequence. North is toward the top of the frame as presented in the EO animation.

blocks.html: Researchers using ASTER and COSI-Corr co-registration report average migration in this region on the order of ~7–32 meters per year, with large dunes near ~9 m/yr and some smaller dunes much faster — locally reported up to ~83 m/yr. Forms can persist while positions shift; smaller dunes may appear and vanish.

The southern Namib is a high-energy wind regime. Dark barchan trains march northward along sand-transport pathways feeding the Namib Sand Sea. That combination — persistent wind, measurable rates, and a clean satellite record — is why this location clears an evidence gate that a generic “dunes move” essay would fail.

blocks.caption: Southern Namibia — Sperrgebiet corridors between coastal sand sources and the Namib Sand Sea.

sections.heading: Grain by grain — not a sliding pile

blocks.html: A dune does not skate across the desert as a solid object. Wind lifts and hops grains on the windward slope (saltation), eroding that face. Grains crest and avalanche down the lee slip face. Redeposition advances the form. Repeat endlessly and the landform migrates while the sand inventory turns over.

blocks.alt: Cross-section of a barchan showing windward erosion, saltation, slip-face deposition, and a later crest position

blocks.html: Size matters: larger dunes often move more slowly and keep their outline; smaller ones can race — and sometimes disappear between annual scenes.

sections.heading: What the satellites do not invent

blocks.html: These frames are evidence of displacement in a published, registered sequence — not a decorative wipe on one photo. Rates quoted here come from peer-reviewed remote-sensing work and NASA EO’s summary of that research, not from hand-measuring pixels on this page.
Other deserts host migrating dunes. This corridor simply offers one of the clearest public demonstrations: same geography, years apart, motion you can see.
